passage_text: Researchers studied the effects of a novel anti-inflammatory drug on joint pain in patients with rheumatoid arthritis. The study was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial conducted over 12 weeks. A total of 200 participants were enrolled and assigned to one of four groups: placebo, low dose (25 mg), medium dose (50 mg), or high dose (100 mg). Pain was assessed weekly using a standardized visual analog scale (VAS) ranging from 0 (no pain) to 100 (worst pain). At the end of the trial, mean VAS scores and standard deviations were recorded for each group. The data are summarized in Table 1 below. The investigators hypothesized that higher doses would produce greater reductions in pain scores. They also planned to analyze the safety profile by recording adverse events. The results showed a clear dose-response trend, with the high-dose group reporting the greatest average pain reduction. However, the incidence of mild gastrointestinal upset increased with dose. These findings suggest that while the drug is effective, dosing must balance efficacy with tolerability.
stem: Which treatment group had the lowest mean VAS score at the end of the trial?
explanation: The high-dose group reported the greatest pain reduction, reflected by the lowest mean VAS score of 25.
trap: Choosing the placebo group because it has the highest pain score, forgetting that a lower VAS score means less pain.

stem: Which of the following is an appropriate control group for this study?
explanation: Correct: A placebo group has the same procedures as the drug groups without the active drug, so it is the control for comparing drug effects. Why the others are wrong: B) the low dose is an active treatment arm. C) the high dose is an active treatment arm. D) healthy volunteers differ from the patients in the disease being studied, so they are not a valid comparison.
trap: Choosing an active-dose group or a non-arthritic group as the control, when the comparison needs patients with the same disease receiving an inactive treatment.

trap: Reporting the 15-point difference as 15% instead of dividing by the starting low-dose score of 55.

stem: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the data presented?

options.A: Higher doses produce greater pain reduction.
options.B: Incidence of mild gastrointestinal upset increases with dose.
options.C: Low dose is more effective than placebo.
options.D: High dose has the highest mean VAS score.

explanation: The high-dose group actually has the lowest mean VAS score, not the highest.
trap: Reading 'highest' as the better outcome; on a pain scale the high-dose group's lowest VAS score means the greatest pain reduction.

stem: By how many VAS points was the high-dose group's mean score lower than the placebo group's?
explanation: Correct: 70 - 25 = 45 VAS points. Why the others are wrong: A) 15 is the step between adjacent dose groups, not high dose versus placebo. B) 30 is the placebo versus medium-dose difference (70 - 40). D) 95 adds the two means instead of subtracting.
trap: Using the step between adjacent dose groups (15) or adding the means (95) instead of subtracting high dose from placebo.
